classification.difficultyReason: Connects circumference, diameter and radius across four dependent calculations, including interpreting the gap as a difference of radii.

content.prompt:
Imagine that we wrapped a belt tightly around the equator of a spherical model of the Earth.
This belt would touch the model at all points on its circumference.

children.label: a
children.prompt: If the diameter of the model is 12 755 metres, calculate to 2 decimal places the length of the tight belt.

questionDiagrams.retentionReason: Complex illustrative raster of a globe with irregular continents, curved belt, buckle, overlap and photographic shading. It contains no mathematical labels or dimensions; native reconstruction would change the supplied illustration.

children.label: b
children.prompt:
Now suppose we added one extra metre to the length of the belt.
Suppose the longer belt forms a circle centred on the model, leaving an equal gap all the way around.
Add 1 metre to the length of the tight belt. What is its length? Give your answer to 2 decimal places, using the unrounded belt length from part a.

children.label: c
children.prompt: Calculate the diameter of the longer, looser belt. Give your answer to 2 decimal places.

children.label: d
children.prompt: What is the gap between the model and the loose belt? Give your answer in metres to 2 decimal places.

answer.short: $0.16\text{ m}$; half the difference of the diameters.
answer.worked:
The gap is half the difference of the two diameters.
$$\begin{align*}g&=\frac{d_{\text{loose}}-12\,755}{2}\\g&=\frac{\frac{12\,755\pi+1}{\pi}-12\,755}{2}\\g&\approx0.16\text{ m}\end{align*}$$
